questions.q: In the champion/challenger pattern, what does "challenger" refer to?
options: A model version that has already failed evaluation
A candidate model version being evaluated to possibly replace the currently live model
The oldest model version in the registry
A model trained on a different company's data
questions.explain: The challenger is a candidate competing to take over from the champion, the version currently serving real traffic.

questions.q: Why must a challenger be compared to the champion on the exact same fixed holdout set?
options: Because MLflow requires it technically
So the comparison is fair — a different sample or time window could make a worse model look better by chance
Because holdout sets expire after one use
Because the registry won't allow multiple runs otherwise
questions.explain: An apples-to-apples comparison requires evaluating both models against the identical evaluation data, not different samples.

questions.q: What is the defining feature of shadow deployment?
options: The challenger serves 50% of all production traffic
The challenger makes real predictions on live traffic, but those predictions are only logged, never served or acted on
The challenger is deployed to a separate, disconnected test environment
The challenger replaces the champion immediately with no further testing
questions.explain: Shadow deployment lets a team observe how a challenger behaves on real traffic with zero user-facing risk, since its predictions are never actually used.

questions.q: What distinguishes a canary rollout from shadow deployment?
options: A canary rollout happens before any offline comparison at all
In a canary rollout, the challenger's predictions actually serve a small percentage of real traffic and count for real
A canary rollout never increases its traffic percentage
Canary rollout and shadow deployment are the same thing
questions.explain: Unlike shadow deployment (logged but unused predictions), a canary rollout lets the challenger's predictions actually affect a small, real slice of production decisions.

questions.q: Why is the actual promotion step (reassigning the champion alias) deliberately a single, trivial line of code?
options: Because MLflow does not support more complex promotion logic
So that all the real risk and decision-making happens in the comparison stages beforehand, not in the promotion action itself
Because aliases cannot be changed more than once
Because promotion should always be fully automatic with no human review
questions.explain: Making the mechanical act of promotion trivial (one alias reassignment) is intentional — it pushes all the real evaluation work into the offline, shadow, and canary stages that come before it.
